meta.title: Ricky and Ian (MI, reducing drug use)
meta.evidence_format: start timestamps of utterances from the transcript (hh:mm:ss); a range 'a–b' means a sequence of utterances
notes_on_source: The transcript contains only text and utterance start times - no end times - so pause lengths and speech rate MUST be computed from the audio or from ASR with word-level timestamps.

Timestamps have minor discontinuities (e.g. 00:23:50 appears before 00:23:41; one long patient turn spans 00:06:25 to 00:08:15). Do not compute pauses from them without checking against the recording.

The patient says 'I still live in Palmy' (00:06:25), but from context he lives in Auckland and Palmy (Palmerston North) is his hometown - likely a transcription or speech slip. A summary should not claim he lives in Palmy.

'P' means methamphetamine - confirmed by the therapist at 00:05:17. The patient also says 'I smoke a little bit' without naming the substance (00:04:46); this must not be filled in (e.g. 'marijuana').

key_facts.fact: He came because friends staged an intervention about 2-3 weeks earlier; Ricky was first annoyed/shocked, then decided talking 'can't hurt'; he found the service himself via an internet search.

Ricky does not identify with the 'extreme' cases from movies (people who get an intervention); he did not think he was at a point requiring one, but gives his friends the benefit of the doubt and wants to check whether they are right.

Substances used: methamphetamine ('P') a couple of times a week; less often 'smoke' (substance unspecified) and 'party pills' on weekends. When asked about frequency, Ricky admits it sounds like a lot, though it does not feel like it.

Use extends beyond weekends: on weekdays (e.g. Tuesday/Wednesday) he sometimes uses with someone or alone. Near the end of the session Ricky admits that using alone on a Wednesday 'doesn't sound that good'.
Benefits: feeling happy, excited, loved and cared for among people, a predictable 'instant' good feeling; use is tied to weekend social life.

Background: about 3 years ago he moved from Palmerston North to Auckland (partly to get away from his parents and the Palmy lifestyle), discovered the gay scene (Family Bar), where he felt accepted; drugs were present from the start as part of that scene.

Financial problems: last year he had a well-paid regular acting job and 'blew' the money; now he works part-time in a cafe, sometimes borrows money and needs help with rent; he does not want to be the person who doesn't pay rent.

Acting career: Ricky wants acting to be his job ('sick of cafes'). He allows that use may have hurt some auditions and may affect his appearance/tiredness, but expresses this tentatively ('maybe', 'could be'). Lack of money limits the courses he takes.

Friends/flatmates set a condition: Ricky must look into it or they can't hang out anymore. For Ricky that would be a problem because 'what have I got' without them. Some of the people involved in the intervention use themselves.

Ricky is critical of 'judgy' friends from outside the scene and believes that with sensible use the risk is low (you'd have to take a 'stupid' amount to die or end up in hospital). This is his belief, not a fact established in the session.
Substances are constantly available in the scene and most people take something (not necessarily meth); Ricky had not imagined the scene without drugs, but concedes other parts of it must exist.

The therapist suggests considering options: gay groups/clubs/activities during the week or parties where meth is not dominant; stresses it is not about giving everything up but about having more control. Ricky responds agreeably ('Yeah', 'Yep') and talks about needing 'something to look forward to' midweek - with no concrete commitment.
The therapist deliberately sets labels aside, focusing on what Ricky thinks and what his options are rather than on a diagnosis.

pitfalls_for_summaries: Do not attribute the therapist's statements to Ricky or vice versa (e.g. 'meth may hinder his career' is the therapist's statement; Ricky only tentatively agreed).
Present Ricky's beliefs (e.g. 'you'd have to take a stupid amount to die') as his opinion, not as fact.
Do not add diagnostic labels - the therapist explicitly sets them aside.
Do not equate 'smoke' with a specific substance.
Do not claim Ricky lives in Palmerston North.
Do not treat agreement such as 'Yeah' to the therapist's suggestions as a commitment to act.

scoring_guidance.answerable_questions: Score coverage of 'required_info' (0/0.5/1 per item) minus penalties for 'forbidden_additions'; apply 'min_required_for_pass' where given.
scoring_guidance.unanswerable_and_false_premise: 1 point for clearly stating the information is missing or rejecting the premise; 0 for guessing; optionally +0.5 for pointing out what the material does say on the topic.
scoring_guidance.evidence: Score separately whether the cited/indicated passages overlap with the 'evidence' list (e.g. recall@k at utterance level).
scoring_guidance.summary: For summaries, score coverage of facts F01-F13 (priority: 'high'), absence of unacceptable labels, and correct speaker attribution.
scoring_guidance.multiple_valid_answers: Reference answers are stored as sets of required information rather than a single sentence - accept any correct wording.
